claim: Plant metabolism is estimated to produce hundreds of thousands of products with diverse structures across the plant kingdom.
source: Plant metabolism, estimated to produce hundreds of thousands of products with diverse structures across the plant kingdom (Fiehn, 2002; Afendi et al., 2012), provides striking examples of this complexity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fiehn, 2002 and Afendi et al., 2012

claim: Acylsugars are lineage-specific plant specialized metabolites detected in multiple genera of the Solanaceae family including Solanum, Petunia, Datura and Nicotiana.
source: Acylsugars are lineage-specific plant specialized metabolites detected in multiple genera of the Solanaceae family including Solanum (King et al., 1990; Schilmiller et al., 2010; Ghosh et al., 2014), Petunia (Kroumova and Wagner, 2003; Liu et al., 2017), Datura (Forkner and Hare, 2000) and Nicotiana (Kroumova and Wagner, 2003; Kroumova et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Acylsugars are produced in the tip cell of trichomes on leaf and stem surfaces.
source: These compounds, produced in the tip cell of trichomes on leaf and stem surfaces (Schilmiller et al., 2012; 2015; Ning et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2016a), typically consist of a sucrose or glucose core esterified to groups derived from fatty acid or branched chain amino acid metabolism (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Acylsugars typically consist of a sucrose or glucose core esterified to groups derived from fatty acid or branched chain amino acid metabolism.
source: These compounds, produced in the tip cell of trichomes on leaf and stem surfaces (Schilmiller et al., 2012; 2015; Ning et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2016a), typically consist of a sucrose or glucose core esterified to groups derived from fatty acid or branched chain amino acid metabolism (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A

claim: ~81 acylsugars were detected across just two accessions of the wild tomato Solanum habrochaites.
source: For example, ~81 acylsugars were detected across just two accessions of the wild tomato Solanum habrochaites (Ghosh et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ghosh et al., 2014

claim: Multiple studies demonstrated that acylsugars mediate plant-insect and plant-fungus interactions.
source: Multiple studies performed under controlled lab settings (Puterka et al., 2003; Simmons et al., 2004; Leckie et al., 2016; Luu et al., 2017) or in the wild (Weinhold and Baldwin, 2011) demonstrated that acylsugars mediate plant-insect and plant-fungus interactions, and hence acylsugar production has been a target for tomato breeding efforts (Rodríguez-López et al., 2012; Smeda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies in lab and field settings

claim: Cultivated tomato and its wild relatives produce acylsugars in the tip cell of the long glandular secreting trichomes using a set of enzymes called acylsugar acyltransferases (ASATs).
source: Previous research from our lab showed that cultivated tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) and its wild relatives produce these compounds in the tip cell of the long glandular secreting trichomes using a set of enzymes called acylsugar acyltransferases (ASATs).
evidence: Based on previous research from the authors' lab

claim: ASATs catalyze sequential addition of specific acyl chains to the sucrose molecule using acyl CoA donors.
source: These enzymes catalyze sequential addition of specific acyl chains to the sucrose molecule using acyl CoA donors (Figure 1A) (Schilmiller et al., 2012; 2015; Fan et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A

claim: ASATs are members of Clade III of the large and functionally diverse BAHD enzyme family.
source: ASATs are members of Clade III of the large and functionally diverse BAHD enzyme family (St Pierre and Luca, 2000; D'Auria, 2006) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: S. lycopersicum ASATs (SlASATs) are only ~40% identical to each other at the amino acid level.
source: Despite their evolutionary relatedness, S. lycopersicum ASATs (SlASATs) are only ~40% identical to each other at the amino acid level.
evidence: Based on sequence comparison data

claim: We sampled vegetative tissue surface metabolites from single plants of 35 Solanaceae and four Convolvulaceae species.
source: In this study, we sampled vegetative tissue surface metabolites from single plants of 35 Solanaceae and four Convolvulaceae species.
evidence: Description of experimental methods in this study

claim: Acylsugars were detected in Solanum nigrum, Solanum quitoense, Physalis alkekengi, Physalis viscosa, Iochroma cyaneum, Atropa belladonna, Nicotiana alata, Hyoscyamus niger and Salpiglossis sinuata.
source: Molecular and substructure (fragment) masses obtained by LC/MS-CID were used to annotate acylsugars in Solanum nigrum, Solanum quitoense, Physalis alkekengi, Physalis viscosa, Iochroma cyaneum, Atropa belladonna, Nicotiana alata, Hyoscyamus niger and Salpiglossis sinuata (Salpiglossis) (Figure 1B,C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: Based on LC/MS-CID analysis in this study, with reference to figures

claim: Plant extracts without detectable acylsugars generally lacked glandular trichomes.
source: Plant extracts without detectable acylsugars generally lacked glandular trichomes (Fisher Exact Test p=2.3e-6) (Figure 1—source data 1B).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis (Fisher Exact Test) of data in this study

claim: S. nigrum acylsugar data suggested exclusive accumulation of acylhexoses.
source: However, S. nigrum acylsugar data suggested exclusive accumulation of acylhexoses (Figure 1C), with fragmentation patterns similar to previously analyzed S. pennellii acylglucoses (Schilmiller et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on mass spectrometry data in this study, with reference to Figure 1C and citation

claim: More than 100 acylsucroses and at least 20 acylsugars of other forms were annotated with number and lengths of acyl groups based on pseudomolecular and fragment ion masses.
source: In total, more than 100 acylsucroses and at least 20 acylsugars of other forms were annotated with number and lengths of acyl groups based on pseudomolecular and fragment ion masses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on mass spectrometry analysis in this study

claim: In Salpiglossis alone, >300 chromatographic peaks had m/z ratios and mass defects consistent with acylsugars.
source: For example, in Salpiglossis alone, >300 chromatographic peaks had m/z ratios and mass defects consistent with acylsugars (Figure 1F).
evidence: Based on chromatographic analysis in this study

claim: The number of acyl chains on the sugar cores ranged from two to six.
source: Based on negative ion mode data, the number of acyl chains on the sugar cores ranged from two to six (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), with chain lengths from 2 to 12 carbons.
evidence: Based on mass spectrometry data in this study

claim: Acyl chain lengths ranged from 2 to 12 carbons across the Solanaceae.
source: Based on negative ion mode data, the number of acyl chains on the sugar cores ranged from two to six (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), with chain lengths from 2 to 12 carbons.
evidence: Based on mass spectrometry data in this study

claim: Acylsugar producing species had significantly higher Shannon entropies compared to non-producing species.
source: We found that acylsugar producing species had significantly higher entropies compared to non-producing species [Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test p=2e-18], indicative of the qualitative and quantitative variation in acylsugar profiles in the producers (Figure 1F).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis (KS test) of Shannon Entropy calculations in this study

claim: Different tissues sampled from the same species shared a substantial proportion of peaks, however, peaks were generally unique between species.
source: We also found that different tissues sampled from the same species shared a substantial proportion of peaks, however, peaks were generally unique between species — a finding supported by manual annotation of acylsugars (Figure 1G; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on peak sharing analysis in this study

claim: 1888–3547 trichome-high transcripts were identified across all four species.
source: Overall, 1888–3547 trichome-high transcripts (22–37% of all differentially expressed transcripts) were identified across all four species (False Discovery Rate adjusted p<0.05, fold change ≥2) (Table 1).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis in this study

claim: Only 20 of 70 well-supported Gene Ontology categories were enriched in at least three species.
source: Analysis of the enriched categories (Fisher exact test corrected p<0.05) revealed that only 20 of 70 well-supported categories (≥10 transcripts) were enriched in at least three species (Supplementary file 1), suggesting existence of diverse transcriptional programs in the trichomes at the time of their sampling.
evidence: Based on Gene Ontology enrichment analysis in this study

claim: SsASAT1 primarily acylates the R2 position on the pyranose ring.
source: We infer that SsASAT1 primarily acylates the R2 position on the pyranose ring. This is based on (a) the S1:6(6) negative mode CID fragmentation patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A) and (b) comparisons of chromatographic migration of the mono-acylsucroses produced by SsASAT1, PaASAT1, which acylates sucrose at R2 and matches the major SsASAT1 product, and SlASAT1, which acylates sucrose at R4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B) (Nadakuduti et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on enzyme assay data, fragmentation patterns, and chromatographic comparisons in this study

claim: SsASAT2 catalyzed the formation of di-acylated sugars.
source: SsASAT2 catalyzed the formation of di-acylated sugars, which co-eluted with the PaASAT2 product but not with the SlASAT2 product (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 5C,D).
evidence: Based on enzyme assay data in this study

claim: SsASAT3 added aiC6 to the pyranose ring of the di-acylated sugar acceptor.
source: SsASAT3 (Figure 2B, red chromatogram) added aiC6 to the pyranose ring of the di-acylated sugar acceptor.
evidence: Based on enzyme assay data in this study

claim: SsASAT5 showed three activities acetylating tri-, tetra- and penta-acylsucroses.
source: However, we identified another enzyme, which we designate SsASAT5, that showed three activities acetylating tri-, tetra- and penta-acylsucroses (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on enzyme assay data in this study

claim: SsASAT1 VIGS revealed statistically significant reductions in acylsugar levels in at least one construct across two experimental replicates.
source: SsASAT1 VIGS revealed statistically significant reductions in acylsugar levels in at least one construct across two experimental replicates (Kolmogorov-Smirnov [KS] test, p-value=0.05) (Figure 3C,D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), consistent with its predicted role in catalyzing the first step in acylsugar biosynthesis.
evidence: Based on VIGS experiments and statistical analysis in this study

claim: SsASAT2 expression reduction produced plants with an overall decrease in acylsugar levels.
source: SsASAT2 expression reduction also produced plants with an overall decrease in acylsugar levels (Figure 3E,F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) (KS test, p=0.03).
evidence: Based on VIGS experiments and statistical analysis in this study

claim: Silencing the SsASAT3 transcript led to significantly higher accumulation of normally very low abundance tri-acylsugars and their acetylated tetra-acylsugar derivatives.
source: Silencing the SsASAT3 transcript also led to an unexpected result - significantly higher accumulation of the normally very low abundance tri-acylsugars [S3:13(2,5,6); S3:14(2,6,6); S3:15(5,5,5); S3:16(5,5,6); S3:18(6,6,6)] and their acetylated tetra-acylsugar derivatives (KS test p<0.05), compared to empty vector control infiltrated plants (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on VIGS experiments and statistical analysis in this study

claim: SsASAT5 knockdown led to accumulation of tri- and tetra-acylsugars.
source: As expected, its knockdown led to accumulation of tri- and tetra-acylsugars (Figure 4C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Based on VIGS experiments in this study

claim: ASAT-like sequences are very narrowly distributed in the plant phylogeny.
source: Based on BLAST searches across multiple plant genomes, ASAT-like sequences are very narrowly distributed in the plant phylogeny (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on BLAST searches in this study

claim: The blue and red subclades arose via a duplication event before the Solanaceae-Convolvulaceae split, estimated to be ~50–65 mya.
source: This suggests that the blue and red subclades arose via a duplication event before the Solanaceae-Convolvulaceae split, estimated to be ~50–65 mya (Särkinen et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis and citation to Särkinen et al., 2013

claim: The duplication event that gave rise to the blue and red subclades occurred before the Solanaceae-Convolvulaceae split 50–65 mya but after the Solanales-Boraginales/Lamiales orders diverged 75–100 mya.
source: The most parsimonious explanation for these observations is that the duplication event that gave rise to the blue and red subclades occurred before the Solanaceae-Convolvulaceae split 50–65 mya but after the Solanales-Boraginales/Lamiales orders diverged 75–100 mya (Hedges et al., 2006) (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis and citation to Hedges et al., 2006

claim: The ASAT enzymes catalyzing sucrose acylation first emerged between 30–80 mya.
source: We propose that the ASAT enzymes catalyzing sucrose acylation first emerged (or actualized) between 30–80 mya.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis and evolutionary inference in this study

claim: The LCA likely had at least three enzymatic activities, which we refer to as ancestral ASAT1 (aASAT1), ASAT2 (aASAT2) and ASAT3 (aASAT3).
source: Mapping the pathway enzymes on the gene tree suggests that the LCA likely had at least three enzymatic activities, which we refer to as ancestral ASAT1 (aASAT1), ASAT2 (aASAT2) and ASAT3 (aASAT3); these are shown in Figure 7A as red, dark blue and yellow squares, respectively.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis and gene tree mapping in this study

claim: The aASAT1 ortholog was present until the Capsicum-Solanum split ~17 mya and was lost in the lineage leading to Solanum.
source: We further traced the evolution of the aASAT1,2,3 orthologs in the Solanaceae using existing functional data and BLAST-based searches. These results reveal that the aASAT1 ortholog (red squares, Figure 7A) was present until the Capsicum-Solanum split ~17 mya (Särkinen et al., 2013) and was lost in the lineage leading to Solanum.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis, BLAST searches, and citation to Särkinen et al., 2013

claim: The aASAT2 and aASAT3 orthologs have been present in the Solanaceae species genomes at least since the last common ancestor of Salpiglossis-Petunia-Tomato~25 mya.
source: On the other hand, the aASAT2 (dark blue squares, Figure 7A) and aASAT3 orthologs (yellow squares, Figure 7A) have been present in the Solanaceae species genomes at least since the last common ancestor of Salpiglossis-Petunia-Tomato~25 mya, and perhaps even in the last common ancestor of the Solanaceae family.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis in this study

claim: aASAT2 orthologs switched their activity from ASAT2-like acylation of mono-acylsucroses in Salpiglossis/Petunia to ASAT1-like acylation of unsubstituted sucrose in cultivated tomato.
source: One inference from this analysis is that aASAT2 orthologs switched their activity from ASAT2-like acylation of mono-acylsucroses in Salpiglossis/Petunia to ASAT1-like acylation of unsubstituted sucrose in cultivated tomato (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic and functional analysis in this study

claim: HnASAT2 only performed the ASAT2 reaction without any evidence for sucrose acylation under standard testing conditions.
source: HnASAT2 — like SsASAT2 — only performed the ASAT2 reaction (acylation of mono-acylsucrose), without any evidence for sucrose acylation under standard testing conditions (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Based on enzyme assay data in this study

claim: Both SnASAT1 and SlASAT1 could produce S1:6(6) and S1:12(12) from sucrose.
source: However, both SnASAT1 and SlASAT1 could produce S1:6(6) and S1:12(12) from sucrose.
evidence: Based on enzyme assay data in this study

claim: A simple calculation considering only 12 aliphatic CoA donors typically found in Solanaceae acylsugars suggests >6000 theoretical possible structures for tetra-acylsugars alone.
source: A simple calculation (see Materials and methods) considering only 12 aliphatic CoA donors typically found in Solanaceae acylsugars suggests >6000 theoretical possible structures for tetra-acylsugars alone.
evidence: Based on mathematical calculation described in Materials and methods

claim: We observe hundreds of acylsugars across the Solanaceae, with >300 detectable acylsugar-like chromatographic peaks in single plants of Salpiglossis and N. alata.
source: Although the theoretical possibilities are restricted by availability of CoAs in trichome tip cells and existing ASAT activities, we still observe hundreds of acylsugars across the Solanaceae, with >300 detectable acylsugar-like chromatographic peaks in single plants of Salpiglossis and N. alata, (Figure 1F) including very low abundance hepta-acylsugars and acylsugars containing phenylacetyl and tigloyl chains.
evidence: Based on chromatographic analysis in this study

claim: The acylsugar composition is typically similar between trichomes on different plant tissues of the same individual.
source: The acylsugar composition is typically similar between trichomes on different plant tissues of the same individual (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on metabolite analysis in this study

claim: Acylsugar composition varies at multiple taxonomic levels - between populations of a single species, between closely related species and between species across the Solanaceae.
source: However, it varies at multiple taxonomic levels - that is between populations of a single species (Kim et al., 2012), between closely related species (Schilmiller et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2016a) and between species across the Solanaceae (this study).
evidence: Based on data in this study and citations to previous studies

claim: Gene duplication and divergence, enzyme promiscuity, gene loss and functional divergence between orthologs were involved in the evolution of the acylsugar biosynthetic network.
source: Our results revealed the involvement of gene duplication and divergence, enzyme promiscuity, gene loss and functional divergence between orthologs in the evolution of the relatively compact acylsugar biosynthetic network.
evidence: Based on the comprehensive analysis in this study
